archetype.name: Rebuilding
archetype.definition: A team in its third straight season near the bottom of the site's rankings, getting badly outplayed at 5-on-5 while it gives heavy minutes to a lineup that isn't yet winning its matchups.

report.headline: Outshot and out-chanced nightly: another bottom-tier season is taking shape
report.take:
Chicago is 3-8-0 and 31st of 32 on the site, and the record is not lying. The goal differential of -19 (24 scored, 43 allowed) ranks 31st per game, and Pts vs Goal Diff sits at -0.5. That means the Blackhawks aren't losing a pile of coin-flip games they should have split. They are getting beaten, usually by more than a goal.

The root problem is territory. Chicago takes 21.4 shots a game, 31st in the league and six fewer than the league average, while allowing 30.4, 28th. At 5-on-5 it owns 40.3% of the expected goals and 41% of the shot attempts, both bottom-three. The power play makes it worse: it converts 8.3%, dead last against a league average of 21.2%. A team that rarely has the puck and can't punish penalties has almost no path to goals. Scoring 2.18 a game, 31st, is what that produces. Both Forwards and Defense grade F.

The numbers hide some bad luck, but not enough to change the story. Five-on-5 PDO is 97.9, the skaters shoot 10.2% against a league 11.3%, and the team save percentage of .880 trails the league's .892. Some of that will drift back. Much of the save-percentage damage, though, comes from Arvid Soderblom's two starts (.820, -2.8 GSAx). Spencer Knight has been close to average at .891. Normal luck would turn a very bad team into a bad one, not a competitive one.

History confirms this is the baseline rather than a slump. The last two seasons finished at 61 and 72 points with xGF % of .431 and .424, so this year's .403 is the same team, a little worse at controlling play. The last five games (2-3-0, allowing 3.4 a game against 3.91 for the season) show a slightly tighter defense. That is a small, mostly home-ice sample. The direction of the season depends on whether the top of the lineup starts winning minutes, and so far it is losing them badly.

strengths.title: Knight keeping games within reach
strengths.body: Spencer Knight has started nine of eleven games and owns a .891 save %, essentially the league's .892 team average. His -1.2 GSAx is only modestly below expected, which is remarkable given he faces 30-plus shots a night. This is the one group not graded F. As long as he carries the starts, most losses should stay competitive rather than turning into blowouts.

strengths.title: Depth lines breaking even
strengths.body: The lower-minute forwards are the only skaters who win or tie their 5-on-5 chance battle. Ryan Greene sits at a .529 xGF %, Cole Smith at .508, and Jordan Greenway at .474, each with a plus-minus between 0 and +1. They aren't producing points, but they are not the reason Chicago gets caved in. It suggests the matchup problem sits higher in the lineup, not throughout it.

concerns.title: Chronic loss of territory
concerns.body: Chicago takes 41% of the 5-on-5 shot attempts and 40.3% of the expected goals, both near the league floor. Its shot totals for and against are a mirror of a team that defends in its own zone most nights. This isn't new: xGF % was .431 and .424 the last two years. It is structural and unlikely to fix itself in-season.

concerns.title: A power play that isn't scoring
concerns.body: At 8.3% the power play ranks 32nd, far under the league's 21.2%. The whole forward group has only 4 power-play points. Some of this is small-sample bad luck and should creep upward; last season's unit ran at 16.9% and the year before at 24.9%. For a team that struggles to generate at even strength, though, it removes the most realistic route to offense.

concerns.title: Top minutes getting buried
concerns.body: The forwards playing the most are losing the worst. Patrick Kane is -13 with a .341 xGF % in nearly 20 minutes a night. Roman Kantserov (.379), Tyler Bertuzzi (.351) and Anton Frondell (.320) aren't far behind. Behind them, opposing defensemen pile up points at the league's worst rate relative to expectation and take 30.8% of the points against Chicago (the league share is 24.3%), the mark of long shifts pinned in the defensive zone.

trend.note: Losing from the opener in September through October, never stringing more than two wins together. The last five games show slightly fewer goals allowed than the season rate, but the underlying shot share hasn't moved enough to call it a turn.

weekAhead.headline: Two leaky penalty kills, then Boston and Colorado's firepower
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with the softer half. Los Angeles (2-5-2, 30th on the site) comes to Chicago carrying the league's 31st penalty kill at 65.5%. Detroit, the following stop, isn't much better at 65.8%. For a power play converting 8.3%, these are the best chances it will see to get going, and LA's own scoring (29th by Off Rank) gives Knight a manageable night. Detroit is the harder test of the two. The Red Wings own 53.3% of expected goals and take 29.9 shots a game, sixth in the league, which plays straight into Chicago's weakness.

The back half is steep. Boston is 9-2-1 and first on the site, with goaltending at +10.9 GSAx, second in goals against, and a defense holding forwards furthest under expectation of any but one team. That 107.6 PDO will fade eventually, just not necessarily by Halloween. Colorado returns home with Chicago carrying the league's second-best offense and 14% shooting. But the Avalanche's goaltending is -5 GSAx and their defense lets centers outscore expectation (28th), an opening for Frank Nazar and Frondell. Splitting the two LA/Detroit games would be a decent week; anything from Boston is a bonus.

keyMatchups.title: Power play vs. two bad kills
keyMatchups.body: Los Angeles kills 65.5% and Detroit 65.8%, ranked 31st and 30th. Chicago's power play has nowhere to hide this week. If it can't score against these units, the 8.3% is a real problem, not variance.

keyMatchups.title: Boston's hot goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Boston leads the league with +10.9 GSAx and a .925 save %, riding a 107.6 PDO. Against a team that already averages only 21.4 shots, that is close to a worst-case pairing. Chicago needs volume it rarely creates.

keyMatchups.title: Centers against Colorado
keyMatchups.body: Colorado's defense lets centers beat their expected points by 0.8 a game, 28th in the league, behind goaltending graded C-. Nazar, at .477 xGF %, is the Chicago center most likely to cash in.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the power play finally converts against the LA and Detroit penalty kills; it is the one cheap source of goals on the schedule.

restOfSeason.body:
The 82-game pace (22 wins, 45 points) is probably too grim. A 97.9 PDO, sub-league shooting and a historically bad power play all have room to drift toward normal, and Knight should keep taking most of the starts. Expect modest improvement in results, something like a 55 to 68 point finish, landing near last year's 72 only if the power play recovers sharply.

The 5-on-5 game is what won't regress, because it's what this team is. A shot share in the low 40s has held for three seasons, the heaviest-minute forwards are losing their matchups, and both skater groups grade F. Chicago should finish in the league's bottom three. The meaningful questions are internal: whether the top-line minutes start breaking even and whether the blueline stops conceding so much to opposing defensemen.
swingFactors: Power-play conversion recovering toward league average

confidence.note: Only 11 games, but the shot-share profile matches two prior seasons.
